newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Clinton urges Romania to persist in NATO bid.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urges Romania to persist in NATO bid.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton encouraged Romania on Friday to pursue reform and persist in its bid to join NATO, saying the Balkan country was a "beacon of hope" in a turbulent region.

"We're impressed with what you've done. The changes are phenomenal that we've witnessed in such a short period of time," Clinton told Romanian President Emil Constantinescu during a meeting at the presidential Cotroceni Palace.

In central Bucharest, tens of thousands of people gathered in stifling heat in University Square where Clinton, the first U.S. president to visit Romania in 22 years, was to crown his eight-hour stay with an address.

He was certain to tell the mainly young crowd that the door to NATO remained open despite the decision this week in Madrid to limit the Alliance's initial expansion to Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.

At a reception with dozens of Romanian political leaders after the two presidents met, Clinton called Romania "a beacon of hope in a region that has seen so much conflict," Deputy U.S. National Security Adviser James Steinberg told reporters.
Steinberg said that during hour-long talks Constantinescu had stressed to Clinton Romania's efforts to improve ties with its neighbours, including new treaties with Hungary and Ukraine.
Constantinescu, he said, contrasted Romania's stability with turmoil in former Yugoslavia and stressed his country's continuing desire to enter the Western alliance and press ahead with reforms.
He quoted the Romanian president as telling Clinton: "The fact that you have come here is the best commendation for our efforts and the best promise for our future."
Clinton arrived from Poland, where he told a crowd in Warsaw's Castle Square that NATO membership would eliminate the postwar divisions of Europe.
Steinberg said similar enthusiasm in Bucharest showed Romanians were not miffed at Clinton's insistence on limiting the first round of NATO expansion to three.
"A lot of people obviously recognise that the fact that the president felt the answer was 'not yet' was not a reason to have a negative attitude," Steinberg said.
Hundreds of Bucharest residents, many carrying small stars-and-stripes flags, lined roads leading from Otopeni airport after Clinton's late morning arrival.

Although opinion polls show Romanians overwhelmingly support NATO membership, Romania's leaders have accepted the Madrid decision gracefully with expressions of determination to carry on with reform programmes first launched in February.
In addition to its NATO aspirations, Romania wants a "strategic partnership" with Washington.
Steinberg said Clinton had assured Constantinescu that partnership, although no substitute for Romania's interest in NATO, was "an important complement to the NATO effort."

"We believe generally they are on the right track across the board. One of the main reasons that we think they aren't ready yet is that this is a new process and needs to be deepened," the White House official said.
Romania's break with Soviet-style communism was more dramatic and bloody than that experienced by any of the three successful NATO entrants.
More than 1,500 people were killed in the 1989 uprising that overthrew Nicolae Ceausescu, whose 24-year rule grew into one of eastern Europe's harshest Communist regimes.
Clinton's address in Romania was in Bucharest's University Square, where dozens of students were killed in the upheaval.

In the early years of his rule, Ceausescu was lionised by the United States for bucking Soviet-dictated policy in Eastern Europe and two U.S. presidents visited Bucharest -- Richard Nixon in 1969 and Gerald Ford six years later.

At the height of the Cold War, Romania was the sole east European country to have ties with West Germany and it refused to obey Moscow's injunction to sever ties with Israel after the 1967 Six-Day War in the Middle East.
Romania also rejected Moscow's demand to contribute troops to crush Czechoslovakia's 1968 "Prague Spring" of democratic reform.
